query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In an additively manufactured single‐phase FCC Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high‐entropy alloy, degradation at elevated temperatures is primarily governed by enhanced grain-boundary diffusion under oxidizing atmospheres that causes selective oxidation of Ti and Cr. This oxidation leads to the nucleation and growth of continuous, nanometric oxide precipitates along grain boundaries, which in turn embrittle the alloy by compromising intergranular cohesion. In contrast, reducing atmospheres suppress this oxide formation and thereby better preserve mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, FCC-structured high-entropy alloy produced by additive manufacturing, characterized by a refined grain structure and negligible pre-existing intergranular oxide precipitates.
generation.intervention: Thermal exposure at elevated temperature in controlled gas atmospheres, specifically comparing oxidizing (e.g., oxygen-rich) versus reducing (e.g., hydrogen-containing) conditions.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure (approximately 800–1000°C) for a prolonged duration (e.g., around 100 hours) under well-controlled oxidizing or reducing gas environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of Ti- and Cr-rich oxide precipitates along the high-energy grain boundaries of the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation at the grain boundaries drives degradation. Under oxidizing conditions, Ti and Cr at the grain boundaries preferentially form nano-scale oxides, which coalesce into a continuous network that reduces intergranular cohesion and mechanical resilience. Under reducing conditions, this oxidation is suppressed, leading to less damage.
generation.predicted_outcome: Specimens exposed to oxidizing gases will exhibit significantly thicker and more interconnected grain-boundary oxide layers, accompanied by measurable embrittlement and a loss in mechanical properties (e.g., reduced fatigue life and hardness) compared to a baseline (untreated or inert atmosphere). In reducing environments, oxide formation will be minimal and mechanical integrity better retained.
generation.baseline: The untreated or inert atmosphere-exposed condition at the same temperature and duration, where negligible oxide formation and no significant intergranular embrittlement occurs.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic explanation is expected to hold for elevated temperatures (800–1000°C) where diffusion is appreciable and for gas atmospheres with sufficiently high oxidizing or reducing potentials. It may not apply outside these temperature ranges or if other phase instabilities occur.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact contributions of Ti versus Cr oxidation and any potential synergistic effects with other elements in this specific composition. The relative kinetics and spatial distribution of oxide precipitates are not yet quantified for this alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 specimens. Expose identical samples to two rigorous and controlled environments: one oxidizing (e.g., air or an oxygen-rich atmosphere) and one reducing (e.g., an inert gas with a controlled amount of H2) at 900°C for 100 hours. Employ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to characterize grain-boundary oxide formation and use mechanical tests (e.g., Vickers hardness, fatigue testing) to assess integrity.
measurements: Grain-boundary oxide thickness and continuity (via TEM/EDS)
Phase composition of the oxide precipitates
Mechanical property retention (hardness, fatigue life) compared to baseline
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If specimens exposed to oxidizing conditions do not show significantly more extensive grain-boundary oxide formation and associated degradation in mechanical properties compared to those in reducing conditions (or if an alternative microstructural degradation mechanism dominates), then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How do mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering affect the phase evolution, microstructure refinement, and mechanical properties of CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloys?. System: CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy (equimolar or nearly equimolar proportions of Cobalt, Chromium, Iron, Nickel, and Titanium). Processing: Mechanical alloying using a planetary ball mill (QM-1SP4) at 400 rpm for 1–6 hours under argon atmosphere, followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) in a vacuum at 900–1000 °C for 10 minutes with a heating rate of 50 °C/min. Test conditions: Vickers hardness testing at 0.05 kN load with 15 s dwell time; compressive strength tests at a displacement rate of 0.5 mm/min (strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹); XRD analysis with Cu-Kα radiation (2θ range 20°–80°); SEM and TEM for microstructural analysis.
